kid.question: How does the Lord describe His love for Israel?

options.text: A love that is just beginning
A love that lasts forever
A love reserved for the rulers
A love remembered only by ancestors

kid.explanation: The Lord says He has loved Israel with an everlasting love and drawn them with lovingkindness.

kid.question: What will people plant on the mountains of Samaria?

options.text: Vines to grow grapes
Olives to make oil
Wheat to make bread
Flax to make cloth

kid.explanation: The Lord promises that people will plant vines in Samaria and eat what they grow.

kid.question: Who is included among the people coming home?

options.text: Armored soldiers and foreign rulers
Temple guards and royal messengers
Blind people and expectant mothers
Ship captains and traveling merchants

kid.explanation: The returning company includes the blind, the lame, pregnant women, and women giving birth.

kid.question: Which worker pictures the Lord's care for gathered Israel?

options.text: A farmer gathering his grain
A builder repairing his house
A sailor steering his ship
A shepherd guarding his flock

kid.explanation: The Lord who scattered Israel will gather and keep them as a shepherd keeps a flock.

kid.question: What does God promise to change their mourning into?

options.text: Joy as He comforts them
Rest as He brings them home
Peace as He ends the battle
Honor as He restores their wealth

kid.explanation: God promises to comfort His people and turn mourning into joy.

kid.question: What hope is given about the children in the enemy's land?

options.text: They will become the enemy's rulers
They will build a different homeland
They will send their parents payment
They will return to their homeland

kid.explanation: The Lord promises that the children will come again from the enemy's land to their own border.

kid.question: What does Jeremiah 31:21 tell Israel to set up?

options.text: Tents housing the royal guards
Markers showing the road back
Walls surrounding the ruined temple
Stalls selling the temple offerings

kid.explanation: Israel is told to set up waymarks and turn again toward its cities.

kid.question: After pulling down, what does the Lord promise to do?

options.text: Gather and teach again
Heal and feed again
Build and plant again
Guide and protect again

kid.explanation: The Lord says He will watch over them to build and plant, as He previously watched to uproot and destroy.

kid.question: Where will the Lord write His law under the new covenant?

options.text: In His people's hearts
On the city's gates
On the king's crown
In the army's records

kid.explanation: God promises to place His law within His people and write it in their hearts.

kid.question: Where is Jeremiah when Babylon's army surrounds Jerusalem?

options.text: In a camp outside Jerusalem
In the temple's upper room
In the court of the prison
In a house beside Anathoth

kid.explanation: Jeremiah is confined in the prison court while Babylon's army besieges Jerusalem.

high-school.question: How is Israel's restoration connected to God's earlier relationship with them?

options.text: His enduring love draws His people back to Him
Their military success persuades Him to accept them
Their new king establishes their first relationship with Him
Their departure from Egypt ends His obligations to them

high-school.explanation: God identifies Israel as His people and grounds His drawing them in everlasting love and lovingkindness.

high-school.question: How do the route details fit the returning company?

options.text: Coastal harbors and sheltered bays suit returning sailors
Mountain fortresses and concealed roads suit returning soldiers
Market towns and busy crossroads suit returning merchants
Water and an unstumbling way suit vulnerable returning travelers

high-school.explanation: The blind, lame, and expectant mothers are included; God leads by water in a straight way where they will not stumble.

high-school.question: What makes the promised rescue greater than Israel's own resources?

options.text: The neighboring nations provide enough money to buy their freedom
The Lord ransoms them from someone stronger than they are
The returning children overpower the soldiers who captured their parents
The captors voluntarily depart before anyone asks for help

high-school.explanation: The Lord redeems Jacob from the hand of one stronger than Jacob.

high-school.question: How does the watered-garden picture fit the promised return?

options.text: A restricted water supply makes farming replace public worship
The city's gardens become a refuge from continuing foreign rule
Renewed life accompanies provision, comfort, and shared rejoicing
Food production increases while communal sorrow remains unchanged

high-school.explanation: The garden image accompanies abundant provision, singing, comfort, and the turning of mourning into joy.

high-school.question: What response does the Lord make to Ephraim's remorse?

options.text: He demands a military victory before accepting him
He remembers his dear son and promises mercy
He assigns the returning son a different family
He treats instruction as a substitute for compassion

high-school.explanation: Ephraim expresses repentance and shame, and God calls him a dear son whom He still remembers and will have mercy on.

high-school.question: What does the change to the sour-grape saying emphasize?

options.text: People bear responsibility for their own wrongdoing
Children must repeat their parents' religious choices
Parents can remove their children's guilt by confessing
National ancestry determines each person's moral standing

high-school.explanation: The rejected proverb gives way to the statement that each person dies for his own iniquity.

high-school.question: What distinguishes the promised covenant in its description here?

options.text: God's law becomes a set of regulations for foreign captors
God's law becomes a royal privilege withheld from families
God's law becomes an inward commitment of His people
God's law becomes a memorial to the departure from Babylon

high-school.explanation: God contrasts the broken earlier covenant with His law placed within and written on hearts.

high-school.question: How broad is the promised knowledge of the Lord?

options.text: It passes from the priests to the king
It remains among the returning tribal elders
It reaches the rulers of neighboring kingdoms
It extends from the least to the greatest

high-school.explanation: The promise says all will know Him, from least to greatest, and links this with forgiveness.

high-school.question: Why does the promise mention the sun, moon, and stars?

options.text: Their ordered endurance underscores God's commitment to Israel
Their changing brightness predicts the date of Israel's return
Their arrangement assigns each tribe its future territory
Their appearance marks the places where exiles should gather

high-school.explanation: God connects Israel's continued standing before Him with the enduring ordinances of creation.

high-school.question: Why has Zedekiah confined Jeremiah?

options.text: Jeremiah urges the king to abandon the temple ceremonies
Jeremiah announces that Babylon will capture the city
Jeremiah refuses to record the king's military victories
Jeremiah promises that Egypt will overthrow the Chaldeans

high-school.explanation: The king's complaint names Jeremiah's prophecy that God will give Jerusalem to Babylon.

expert.question: What grounds the movement from survival to renewed relationship?

options.text: Survival in the wilderness is credited to a new royal alliance
Rest in the wilderness depends on release from covenant obligations
Return from the wilderness begins a previously unknown divine attachment
Grace in the wilderness is joined to enduring divine love

expert.explanation: The people left from the sword find grace and rest; the following declaration names everlasting love and lovingkindness.

expert.question: How does the route correspond to the composition of the returning group?

options.text: A steep and hidden way protects a company consisting of trained soldiers
Water and an unstumbling way suit a company including vulnerable travelers
A route through foreign capitals suits a company composed of royal envoys
A route without stopping places suits a company separated from its dependents

expert.explanation: The text includes vulnerable travelers and then describes God's leading by rivers along a straight way where they will not stumble.

expert.question: How does the reply to the lament address the reason for weeping?

options.text: It promises the children's return from the enemy's land
It reinterprets the missing children as a successful harvest
It directs the mourners to replace their lost family relationships
It limits the promised restoration to those already within Judah

expert.explanation: Rachel's weeping for her children receives a promise that the children will return from the enemy's land to their border.

expert.question: How does Ephraim's speech interact with the Lord's response?

options.text: Claimed innocence and self-defense receive confirmation of freedom from blame
Requested political independence receives instructions for choosing a different king
Acknowledged discipline and shame meet remembered affection and mercy
Promised material repayment receives a demand for increased sacrificial offerings

expert.explanation: Ephraim confesses chastisement and remorse; God responds by calling him a dear son and promising mercy.

expert.question: What continuity remains through the reversal from destruction to renewal?

options.text: The same foreign ruler administers both the exile and the restoration
The Lord's watchful agency attends both uprooting and rebuilding
The same generation remains untouched by both discipline and restoration
The Lord's watchfulness ends when the people begin rebuilding themselves

expert.explanation: God explicitly parallels His watching to destroy with His watching to build and plant.

expert.question: How does the interpretation revise the allocation of responsibility in the proverb?

options.text: The children's teeth establish the children's duty to avenge their fathers
The fathers' grapes establish the fathers' freedom from personal consequences
The shared vineyard makes each household answer for neighboring households
The eater's own teeth correspond to the eater's own iniquity

expert.explanation: The proverb about fathers eating and children's teeth is replaced by each person's dying for personal iniquity and bearing the sour grape's effect.

expert.question: What does the covenant contrast locate within the renewed relationship?

options.text: An inwardly written law accompanies belonging, knowledge, and forgiveness
A restored ancestral journey replaces the need for inwardly held divine instruction
A new national title replaces the earlier bond between God and His people
A restricted teaching office reserves knowledge of God for the greatest Israelites

expert.explanation: The new covenant combines law in hearts, reciprocal belonging, universal knowledge within the people, and forgiveness.

expert.question: What is the logical force of the condition concerning creation's ordinances?

options.text: Israel's restoration awaits human adjustment of the established cosmic order
Israel's ancestry must be verified by studying the established cosmic order
Israel's rejection is linked to the failure of the established cosmic order
Israel's worship must imitate the movements of the established cosmic order

expert.explanation: God says Israel would cease as a nation before Him if those ordinances departed, stressing the security of His commitment.

expert.question: How does the city's promised holiness extend beyond its usual sacred center?

options.text: It excludes the measured outskirts so that worship remains within the temple
It transfers the city's holiness to a new sanctuary outside the measured area
It includes the valley of bodies and ashes within the restored area's scope
It reserves the renewed city for priests while families settle beyond its gates

expert.explanation: The described area includes the valley of dead bodies and ashes and will be holy to the Lord.

expert.question: What tension frames the transition from restoration promises to Jeremiah's situation?

options.text: Promised rebuilding stands beside a besieged city and an imprisoned prophet
Promised rebuilding follows a completed victory and a newly released prophet
Promised rebuilding is withdrawn when the prophet accepts a royal appointment
Promised rebuilding depends on the prophet denying Babylon's approaching victory

expert.explanation: After promises of restoration, the narrative locates Jeremiah in confinement during the siege because he predicts Babylonian capture.
